subject: physics
question_text: A ball is dropped from the roof of a tall building and simultaneously another ball is thrown horizontally with some velocity from the same roof. Which ball lands first? Explain your answer.

verification.note: Unit 3 has NO Long Answer section in either source book, so no 8-mark form is invented. The Fastrack (pp.6-8) lists 4 Very Short Answer and 6 Short Answer questions plus a PROBLEMS section; the TSBIE Basic Learning Material (pp.4-5) has a Short Answer section ONLY (5 questions) and no VSAQ section. The mark split is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it.

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order. You can speak in English, in Telugu, or in both.

page_header: Motion in a Straight Line · 4 marks

steps.label: The figure
steps.why: Drawing both paths from the same roof to the same ground makes it visible that the two share the same height h and the same vertical start.
common_mistakes: Drawing the thrown ball starting lower than the dropped one. Both leave the same roof.

recall.must_convey: That both balls leave the same roof at height h, one falling straight down and one following a curved path.

steps.memory_tip: Same roof, same h, two paths. The shared h is the point of the picture.
steps.margin_note: Label h once, on the tower.

steps.label: The dropped ball
lines: For the dropped ball, initial vertical velocity
u = 0, acceleration a = g, displacement = h.
From s = ut + ½at²:  h = ½g t₁²
steps.why: Starting from rest removes the ut term, so the whole height is covered by the ½gt² term alone.
common_mistakes: Using v² = u² + 2as when the question asks for a TIME. That equation has no t in it.

recall.must_convey: That for the dropped ball h equals half g t one squared, so t one is root two h by g.
reject: v squared equals u squared plus two a s

steps.memory_tip: Dropped means u = 0, so h = ½gt² and t = √(2h/g).
steps.margin_note: Write u = 0 explicitly. It is why the first term vanishes.

steps.label: The thrown ball
lines: For the thrown ball the VERTICAL motion is
the same: initial vertical velocity uᵧ = 0,
steps.why: A horizontal throw gives the ball horizontal velocity only, so its vertical motion starts from rest exactly like the dropped ball.
common_mistakes: Including the horizontal speed u in the vertical equation. The two directions are independent.

recall.must_convey: That the thrown ball has zero initial vertical velocity, so t two is also root two h by g.

steps.memory_tip: Horizontal and vertical are independent. The throw is all horizontal, so the fall is unchanged.

steps.label: The conclusion

lines.text: t₁ = t₂, so both balls land at the same time

lines: The thrown ball travels further, but it does
not stay in the air any longer.
steps.why: Landing together while covering different distances is what makes this a memorable result, and it is the point the examiner is testing.
common_mistakes: Answering that the dropped ball lands first because its path is shorter. Path length does not set the fall time.

recall.must_convey: That the two times are equal, so both balls land at the same time.

steps.memory_tip: Different distances, same time. Only the vertical motion sets the clock.
steps.margin_note: Answer the question asked: which lands first.

insider_note: Both books ask this. The answer is that they land together — the horizontal throw does not change the vertical fall.
